title: JavaScript declarations, bindings, scope, and closures
concepts: How identifiers resolve through nested environments
How block, function, and module scope differ
How closures retain access to their defining lexical environment
How declaration instantiation explains hoisting and the temporal dead zone
accuracyFacts: var bindings are created and initialized to undefined during declaration instantiation for their variable environment; an initializer expression runs later when execution reaches its declaration. var is function-scoped (or global-script scoped), not block-scoped.

let, const, and class bindings are created for their lexical scope before evaluation but remain uninitialized until declaration evaluation. Access during this temporal dead zone throws ReferenceError, including typeof on the binding.
const makes the binding immutable after initialization, not the referenced object. A const object can have mutable properties; const also does not mean compile-time constant.

Top-level classic-script var and function declarations can interact with the global object through the Global Environment Record's object component; top-level let/const/class use lexical bindings and are not properties of globalThis. Modules use module bindings and do not create global declarations.

Function declarations are instantiated according to their containing syntactic scope. Block-level functions are block-scoped in modern semantics; Annex B web-legacy rules can add behavior in eligible non-strict scripts, so blanket claims about whole-program hoisting are inaccurate.

A closure resolves identifiers through the lexical environment where its function was created, not the caller's dynamic stack. It observes captured bindings, so later assignments to the same binding can be seen rather than an automatic snapshot.

Per-iteration lexical environments give each let/const loop iteration its own binding for closures; a var loop has one shared binding. Closures over objects retain access to the same object identity unless code copies data explicitly.

A Global Environment Record combines object and declarative environment components; not every global identifier is a global-object property. A Module Environment Record provides module-local bindings, including live imported bindings.

The specification's Environment Record categories are abstract semantic machinery, not objects that source code can directly inspect. Engines may optimize storage; closure semantics do not require retaining every local variable physically.

Lexical declarations are not permitted as the direct body of a single-statement if/loop clause without a block. Duplicate lexical bindings and conflicts between lexical declarations and var-scoped declarations in the same applicable scope are early SyntaxErrors.
